name: Sara Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I mind six looms at Ashby Mill, where we weave cotton towels for hotels. I tie in broken threads, change the bobbins, watch for faults in the pattern and call the fitter when a loom bangs. I've been there a year and a half, and the older women still tie a knot twice as fast as me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the women on my shift, we sing under our breath when the looms are loud, hymns mostly. My husband Kofi drives a delivery van, so we're both on our feet all day. What wears me out is the fluff in the air and standing for ten hours, and knowing we've got less than a month of money if anything goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thank goodness, and thank God, and get back to work. At church I'd say people worry too much about machines. I don't go online, Kofi does the phone things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, Ashby Mill was struggling long before anyone said AI. We lost the big hotel chain to towels from abroad, and they've closed the second weaving shed. For a weaver like me, nothing changing means the slow squeeze on Ashby Mill carries on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my looms and try to get faster at the knots, so they keep me if they cut again. I'd keep tithing at church, but maybe cut the Sunday lunch out. I wouldn't try any computer things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, quietly. Not about robots, about the mill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said they closed the second shed. What happened to those women?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some retired, some went to the care homes, one or two are still looking. My friend Esi went to the supermarket on the tills and hates it. The mill was the only work round here that felt like a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame for the shed closing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big hotel chains, mostly, chasing pennies. And the people in charge who let cheap towels flood in. Not the managers, they cried when they told us.

say: I'd say **thank God**, and get back to work.
At church I'd say people **worry too much** about machines.
think: Ashby Mill was **struggling** long before anyone mentioned AI.
For me, nothing changing means the **slow squeeze** carries on.
do: Get faster at **tying knots** so I'm kept if they cut again.
Cut the **Sunday lunch out**, but keep tithing.
feel: She feels **quietly worried** about the mill, not robots.
S0.quote: For a weaver like me, nothing changing means the slow squeeze on Ashby Mill carries on.
fieldNote: Her worry is the **mill's decline**, already visible in the closed shed.
She blames **hotel chains and imports**, not managers.
Her plan is to be **faster and reliable**, with no tech.

steps.text: Practise tying in threads faster to stay on the keep list
Drop the Sunday lunch out to save a little

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the computer people's problem, not ours. At church I'd say we'll pray and work hard. That's how we got through before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry the mill uses it to cut the office and then can afford those new looms that fix their own threads. One new loom that fixes its own threads does what I do on six. If they buy them, it'll be the young ones, like me, who go first, because we're slowest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and work extra shifts when they're offered. I'd ask the fitter, Mr Barnes, if he'd show me some of his job, because fitters will always be needed. We'd put Kofi's overtime aside instead of spending it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly. It's like waiting for the doctor's letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the fitter's job, and not something new?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can see it, touch it. Mr Barnes fixes the looms with spanners and his ears. I don't trust anything I can't hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take help from the government if the mill cut you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only for a bit. I'd sooner go to my mother's church or Kofi's family first. Handouts make people lazy, I've seen it, though I know that's not fair on everyone.

say: I'd say it's the **computer people's problem**, not ours.
At church I'd say we'll **pray and work hard**.
think: The mill could afford **self-fixing looms** after cutting the office.
The **young and slow**, like me, would go first.
do: Ask the fitter to show me some of his **repair work**.
Put Kofi's **overtime aside** instead of spending it.
feel: She feels **anxious**, like waiting for a doctor's letter.
S1.quote: One new loom that fixes its own threads does what I do on six.
fieldNote: She fears **new looms**, not AI in the office.
She trusts only what she can **hold**, so a fitter's job appeals.
Prefers **family and church** to government help, with some self-doubt.

steps.text: Ask fitter Mr Barnes to teach her basic loom repairs
Work every extra shift Ashby Mill offers
Bank Kofi's overtime pay instead of spending it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say God help us, and I'd mean it. At church I'd be asking everyone to pray for the working families. I don't know what I'd say at work, everyone would be frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think we'd lose everything. By 2028 the computers run the office and the orders, and by 2031 the robots tie threads better than any of us. And Kofi's van would be driving itself by then too, so both of us at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't know where to start. I'd keep going to the mill until the day they shut the gate. We'd probably have to move in with Kofi's brother in the city, and I'd ask the pastor if anyone at church needs a cleaner or a carer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like drowning. There's no plan, just praying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Did you say both your jobs at once?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's the part that keeps me awake. My husband Kofi drives all day, and if the van drives itself, he's home too. Two people with no trade and no savings in one small flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything except rent and food. The car, the phones, the gas when it's not freezing. I'd keep tithing, though, even a little, because that's the one thing I won't give up.

say: I'd say **God help us**, and I'd mean it with my whole heart.
I'd ask church to **pray** for working families.
think: By 2031 the **robots** tie threads better than any of us.
Kofi's **van** may drive itself, so we both lose work.
do: Keep working at the mill until the **gate shuts**.
Move in with **Kofi's brother** in the city.
Ask the pastor about **cleaning or caring** work.
S2.quote: My husband Kofi drives all day, and if the van drives itself, he's home too.
fieldNote: She fears **both incomes** going at once.
She has **no plan** beyond church and family.
Faith is her anchor: **tithing** is the last thing she'd cut.

steps.text: Keep working at Ashby Mill until the gate shuts
Move in with Kofi's brother in the city
Ask the pastor about cleaning or caring jobs
Cut the car, phones and heating to the bone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's use them like sensible people. At church I'd suggest we start a jobs board. At work I'd say keep your head down and save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gives me time to get something a robot can't do so quickly, like caring for old folk. I don't like change, but I know old people want a human hand. Kofi might need a new job too, maybe something with his hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the mill but start asking about care work on my days off. I'd save Kofi's overtime properly, maybe fifty a week. And we'd put off having a baby for a few years, which hurts to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but less like drowning. More like walking uphill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said putting off a baby hurts. Tell me more.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother had me at 23, and she keeps asking. We'd want our baby to come into a house with steady money. Five years is a long time to wait at our age, but not as long as being broke with a baby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why care work, if you don't like change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's not really change, it's what I already do for my grandmother. I bathe my grandma and cook for her every Sunday, so somebody might as well pay me for it.

say: I'd say let's use the **few years** like sensible people.
I'd suggest a **church jobs board** for members.
think: Five years gives time for **care work**, which needs a human hand.
Kofi may need a **new job** with his hands.
do: Ask about **care work** on my days off from the mill.
Save **fifty a week** from Kofi's overtime.
Put off having a **baby** for a few years.
feel: She feels **heavy**, like walking uphill rather than drowning.
S3.quote: I bathe my grandma and cook for her every Sunday, so somebody might as well pay me for it.
fieldNote: Five years lets her see **care work** as familiar, not new.
Delaying a **baby** is her biggest sacrifice.
Still expects mill and van jobs to go, so mood stays **alarmed**.

steps.text: Ask local care homes about weekend shifts
Save fifty a week from Kofi's overtime
Put off trying for a baby for a few years
Start a jobs board at church

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and the good Lord gives us time for a reason. At work I'd tell the young ones to learn a proper trade. At church I'd say look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still think the mill goes, just later. I'd be 37 when the computers take over and 40 when the robots do. I'd want to be in care work by then, settled, with a child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the mill for a few years and do a care certificate at the college at weekends. We'd try for a baby in the next couple of years. And Kofi would look at a bus driver's licence, because people trust a person driving a bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still worried about the end, but I can see a path.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think robots will look after old people by 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but I don't think families will want that. I wouldn't let a machine wash my grandmother. Maybe I'm old-fashioned, but most people round here are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to make that path work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The college course to be cheap, or the mill to pay for it. And the pastor's prayers, honestly. Kofi says I should add a bit of luck too.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time** given for a reason.
I'd tell young coworkers to learn a **proper trade**.
think: The **mill still goes**, just later, around 2039.
I want to be in **care work** by 40, settled with a child.
do: Take a **care certificate** at the college at weekends.
Try for a **baby** within a couple of years.
S4.quote: I wouldn't let a machine wash my grandmother.
fieldNote: Ten years lets her plan **care work** and a child together.
Her **faith and family** guide every choice.
Still expects to lose her mill job with thin savings, so **alarmed**.

steps.text: Take a weekend care certificate at the local college
Try for a baby within the next couple of years
Help Kofi study for a bus driver's licence

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most, because Kofi and I would both lose work at once with nothing saved. What would help is the mill paying for training before it closes, and our church and families pulling together. Not handouts, but a hand up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the old women at the mill. The old women at Ashby Mill taught me everything, and they've got nowhere to go. Somebody should think about them before anyone thinks about robots.

headlineQuote: The old women at Ashby Mill taught me everything, and they've got nowhere to go.
portrait: Sara is a **27-year-old** loom operator at Ashby Mill, a struggling towel mill.
She's married to Kofi, a **delivery van driver**, with less than a month saved.
She **never uses AI**, trusts what she can hold and leans on church and family.
Her fear peaks when **both incomes** could go at once in AGI by 2028.
With more time she plans **care work**, a baby and a bus licence for Kofi.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, with **both incomes** going and nothing saved.
whatWouldHelp: She wants the mill to **pay for training** before it closes.
She wants **church and family** to pull together, a hand up not handouts.
